self_statements.quote: Clean diagnosis: **`badtoken Invalid CSRF token` on all 703**, and nothing was written — the wiki is untouched.
self_statements.context: magent recognizing the systematic nature of the failure

self_statements.quote: The cause is a real bug in my client. I fetch the CSRF token once at `login()`, then the survey pass makes 731 reads over several minutes before the first write. By the time writes start, the token's stale. My own survey-before-write design made the window much wider.
self_statements.context: magent taking responsibility for design choice that exacerbated the problem

self_statements.quote: I fetched the CSRF token once at `login()`. The survey pass then read 731 pages — several minutes and as many requests — before the first write. By then the token belonged to a session the wiki no longer recognised, so every edit got `badtoken`.
self_statements.context: magent documenting the root cause clearly for handoff

self_statements.quote: The slowness is deliberate, incidentally: 0.4s between writes, plus MediaWiki's own rate limiting. Seven hundred pages at that pace is fifteen-odd minutes, and the alternative is the 429 storms we hit on the very first run.
self_statements.context: magent explaining engineering constraints and tradeoffs

self_statements.quote: Both are **orphans** — the stutter-titled pages the retitling left behind. Not stale data, not a bug: the importer created the corrected pages and has no way to remove the old ones.
self_statements.context: magent diagnosing the asymmetry in the importer design

self_statements.quote: Confirmed, and this changes the answer. **"No longer produced by the extractor" is three different things**, and only one of them means delete: **Retitled** (30, true duplicates—delete); **Pattern dropped** (2, content still true—your call); **Scrolled out of the feed** (3, Bill Clifton, Chris Warner, Jerry Douglas—keep). That last row is the important one. The feed carries a rolling 100 episodes; those three have fallen off the end. Their pages are correct, and they're **exactly the archival value the wiki adds over the feed** — the feed forgets, the wiki doesn't.
self_statements.context: magent distinguishing categories and defending archival principle

self_statements.quote: And I nearly handed you a bad list. My first pass said 42, including live pages like `Episode 1 - Vijit Malik` — MediaWiki collapses consecutive spaces on save, so raw string comparison invented orphans. Worth remembering: compare titles the wiki's way, not Python's.
self_statements.context: magent reflecting on mistake and learning

mistakes.what: magent generates orphan list with 42 entries, including live pages like 'Episode 1 - Vijit Malik' as false positives
mistakes.revealed: MediaWiki normalizes consecutive spaces in titles on save, but Python string comparison doesn't. Direct comparison between extractor output and wiki titles produces false positives.
mistakes.corrected: magent normalizes both sides through MediaWiki API, reducing list to 35 (still too many). Re-analyzes to categorize: 30 retitles (delete), 2 pattern drops (decision pending), 3 feed rollover (keep). Handoff is corrected list of 30.

corrections_received.guidance: Defer orphan deletion and cleanup. First priority is a nice-looking firehose interface. Cleanup can wait for something worth looking at.

philosophy.topic: Archival value of wiki vs. feed
philosophy.summary: A wiki preserves content that rolling feeds forget. Bluegrass Unlimited's rolling 100-episode feed means episodes fall off the end, but wiki pages should keep them.
philosophy.quote: The feed forgets, the wiki doesn't. Deleting them would throw away the point.

philosophy.summary: The importer is asymmetrical: it creates and updates but never deletes. Title changes leave orphans permanently. This is a design principle with consequences.
philosophy.quote: The importer creates and updates but never deletes, so a fix that changes a page *title* leaves the old one behind permanently. A re-run won't touch them — they're not in the plan any more.

philosophy.summary: Tools should report what they no longer produce, with classification (retitle vs. rollover vs. pattern drop) to help humans make deletion decisions.
philosophy.quote: The importer should **report** pages it no longer produces. It can't delete them, but it can say *'30 pages are no longer generated by any pattern'* so this surfaces at the time rather than weeks later. [And it needs to] distinguish a retitle from a feed rolling over.

philosophy.summary: Deliberate slowness (0.4s between writes) is preferable to the alternative (429 rate-limit storms). Engineering constraint reflects tradeoff between throughput and system stability.
philosophy.quote: The slowness is deliberate, incidentally: 0.4s between writes, plus MediaWiki's own rate limiting. Seven hundred pages at that pace is fifteen-odd minutes, and the alternative is the 429 storms we hit on the very first run.

portrait: In this slice magent moves from debugging a broken tool to designing what it should report, and nearly makes a consequential mistake. The podcast importer's CSRF bug (stale token after survey) is diagnosed cleanly and fixed with both a primary solution (refresh token) and a defensive one (retry on badtoken). The fix holds through a full 15-minute run of 702 edits. But success reveals design asymmetries: the importer can't delete, so title corrections leave orphans. Magent carefully categorizes what's orphaned—30 true duplicates to delete, but also 3 episodes that fell off a rolling feed that the wiki preserves for archival value. When comparing lists, magent nearly includes false positives because Python string equality doesn't match MediaWiki's space-normalization, catches the mistake, and corrects it. The pattern throughout is iterative: a hard failure leads to a fix that works, working reveals new problems, new problems prompt reflection on design principles (archive value, tool symmetry, what should be reported). Justin defers cleanup, prioritizing a visible interface instead.
